keyVerseText: Then said I, Lo, I come (in the volume of the book it is written of me,) to do thy will, O God.
rootMeaning: The word κεφαλίς (kephalís) is a diminutive form of κεφαλή (kephalḗ), meaning 'head.' While κεφαλή refers broadly to the head as the main part or source, κεφαλίς conveys the idea of a 'little head' or an extremity such as the end or knob of an object. This root sense highlights the concept of a prominent or leading end, which metaphorically extends to something like the 'head' or main part of a written volume, rather than simply a physical head on a body.
usageInScripture: This word appears only once in the biblical text, where it is translated as 'the volume' in Hebrews 10:7. Its usage here is consistent with its broader lexical range, which includes meanings such as the capital of a column, the extremity of an object, or the roll of a manuscript. This suggests that κεφαλίς emphasizes the tangible, physical form of a written scroll or book, underscoring the concrete reality of Scripture as a recorded revelation.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding κεφαλίς as the 'volume' or physical roll of a book enriches our appreciation of Scripture as both divine word and tangible record. It reminds believers that God's revelation is not merely abstract but is given in a concrete, accessible form, preserved in writing. This bridges the eternal truth of God's will with the historical reality of the biblical text. Moreover, the connection to 'head' metaphorically points to Christ as the ultimate source and fulfillment of God's will, emphasizing the unity of God's plan revealed in Scripture.
keyVerseReflection: Hebrews 10:7 states, 'Then said I, Lo, I come (in the volume of the book it is written of me,) to do thy will, O God.' The use of κεφαλίς here highlights the authoritative and definitive nature of the written word concerning Christ's mission. It is not a vague promise but a concrete, recorded declaration that Christ fulfills God's will. The term underscores that this revelation is contained within the sacred scroll or volume, affirming the reliability and centrality of Scripture in revealing Christ's purpose.
